Roofing in Cleburne, Texas

Cleburne's older streets and the 2013 tornado both shape how roofs get fixed here. Call one free number, any hour, to reach an independent roofing company that works in Johnson County.

Call (469) 649-7066 Cleburne registration and permits
  1. Home
  2. Service Areas
  3. Cleburne

Cleburne after 9:30 p.m. on May 15, 2013

Ask anyone in Cleburne about roofs and the 2013 tornado comes up quickly. At about 9:30 that night an EF3 tornado moved through the Johnson County seat. The National Weather Service's preliminary survey put its peak winds near 140 mph, its path at about 8.5 miles and its width at roughly 1,060 yards, more than half a mile.

The worst of it fell just east of Lake Pat Cleburne, the reservoir that supplies the city's water. CBS Texas reported that hundreds of homes lost their roofs, debris covered whole blocks, fences were flattened, and about 600 families were affected. The mayor declared a local disaster. It was one of 16 tornadoes the weather service confirmed across North Texas from that outbreak.

Storms have kept coming since. Coverage of a later storm, written around the 13th anniversary of the tornado, reported hail up to 4 inches falling across most of Johnson County and more than 1,000 homes losing power, about half of them in the Cleburne area.

Leave the roof to the roofer. A wet or storm-hit roof is slippery, and damaged decking can give way, so keep off it and keep the ladder put away. Stay clear of any downed power line and report it to Oncor or your local electric utility, or call 911. Inside, pull furniture and electronics away from the drip, set out a bucket or towels, and keep everyone out of a room where the ceiling is sagging. Take photos from the yard and from inside, then call your insurance company and a roofer.

Older roofs in the county seat

Cleburne grew from Camp Henderson, a Civil War mustering point near Buffalo Creek. It became the county seat under its current name, for General Patrick Cleburne, in 1867 and incorporated in 1871. The Santa Fe railroad shops later became its largest employer for about a century, and that history is still visible in the buildings. The Cleburne Downtown Historic District, listed on the National Register, counts 89 contributing buildings from 1877 to 1968. A National Register nomination describes Prairie Avenue as still lined with substantial homes from the late 1800s and early 1900s.

Roofs on houses that old raise questions that newer suburbs rarely face: several layers of old shingles, original board decking, brick chimneys with worn flashing, and porch roofs at a lower pitch than the main roof. A careful roofer looks at all of it before quoting. Cleburne had 31,352 residents at the 2020 census, and plenty of them live in newer neighborhoods too, where the questions are about hail and a first replacement.

What Cleburne requires of a roofer

From the City of Cleburne's Quick Guide to Residential Construction (October 2025) and its Building Inspection FAQ.

  • Every contractor registers. All contractors must be registered with the City of Cleburne before a permit is issued.
  • Re-decking needs a permit. A roofing permit is required for re-decking an existing roof, and only a registered contractor can pull it. The guide lists the roofing (decking only) fee as $30 plus a $20 administrative fee.
  • Every name on the permit. The general contractor and all subcontractors must be registered, current and listed before the permit is issued.
  • 180 days to the first inspection. After that the permit expires and fees must be paid again.
  • Online requests. Permits and inspections run through the city's online portal; inspection requests made before 4 p.m. are scheduled for the next day.

Building Inspections is on the ground floor of City Hall, 10 N. Robinson Street, open Monday through Friday during business hours. Fees can change, so confirm them there. Addresses outside city limits in Johnson County are not under this office.

Before you hire in Cleburne

  1. Get the registered name. Ask what name the company registered under with the City of Cleburne, then confirm it at Building Inspections.
  2. Ask about layers and decking. On an older house, find out how many roofs are already on it and what replacing board or plywood decking will cost per sheet.
  3. Ask who pulls the permit. If decking is replaced, a registered contractor must. Make the fee part of the written price.
  4. Get insurance proof from the source. A certificate sent straight from the insurer is worth more than a photo of one.
  5. Keep your own record. Photos from the ground and inside, dated, help if you file a claim after the next storm.

No state license for roofers. Texas does not license roofing contractors. A 2025 bill that would have had the state license re-roofers (HB 3344) cleared a House committee but never got a floor vote, and it died when the session ended. That puts the checking on you: ask for a certificate of liability insurance sent to you by the roofer's insurance agent or insurer, a written contract that lists the full scope, the permit or contractor registration your city requires, addresses of nearby jobs, and proof the shingle warranty was registered. The line does none of this checking for you. How to check a roofer in Texas.

Your deductible is yours to pay. The Texas Department of Insurance warns that a contractor may not waive your deductible, rebate it, or pad the estimate to cover it, and that a contract of $1,000 or more paid with insurance money must include a notice that you owe the deductible. Your insurer may ask for proof you paid it. A contractor also may not act as a public adjuster on a property it works on or may work on. If a roofer offers to "take care of" the deductible, hire someone else.

A porch roof sagging on an older house, shingles missing after wind, or hail dents along the gutters? Call and describe it. A roofer serving Johnson County takes it from there, sees the house in person and quotes in writing.

What Cleburne homeowners ask about roofing

Do roofing companies in Cleburne TX have to register with the city?

Yes. Cleburne's Quick Guide to Residential Construction says all contractors must be registered with the City of Cleburne. Ask Building Inspections for the current registration fee. The city's FAQ adds that the general contractor and every subcontractor must be registered, current and named on the permit before it is issued. Ask a roofer for the name it registered under and confirm it with Building Inspections at City Hall.

Is a roofing permit required in Cleburne TX?

Cleburne's guide says a roofing permit is required when an existing roof is re-decked, and that only a contractor registered with the city can pull it. The guide does not spell out the rule for a shingle-only job, so ask Building Inspections about yours. Settle in writing who applies for the permit if the crew finds bad decking after tear-off.

What happened in the 2013 Cleburne tornado?

On the night of May 15, 2013, an EF3 tornado with peak winds near 140 mph crossed Cleburne on a path about 8.5 miles long and roughly 0.6 mile wide. CBS Texas reported that hundreds of homes had their roofs torn off and that about 600 families were affected. The heaviest damage was just east of Lake Pat Cleburne.

What should I do first if hail damages my roof in Cleburne?

Stay off the roof. Take dated photos of hail on the ground, dented gutters and anything you can see from the yard, plus any ceiling stains inside. Call your insurer and ask about your wind and hail deductible and the claim deadline. Then have a roofer look. The hail damage page lists what a roofer checks, and the Texas claim guide covers the paperwork.
